source_text: Dixerit aliquis: si nulla est mortuis cura de uiuis, quomodo ille diues, qui apud inferos torquebatur, rogabat Abraham patrem, ut mittat Lazarum ad quinque fratres suos nondum mortuos et agat cum eis, ne ueniant et ipsi in eundem tormentorum locum? sed numquid quia hoc ille diues dixit, ideo quid fratres agerent uel quid paterentur illo tempore sciuit? ita illi fuit cura de uiuis, quamuis quid agerent omnino nesciret, quemadmodum est nobis cura de mortuis, quamuis quid agant utique nesciamus. nam si nihil de mortuis curaremus, non utique pro illis deo supplicaremus. denique Abraham nec Lazarum misit et Moysen ac prophetas hic eos habere respondit, quos audire deberent, ut ad illa supplicia non uenirent. ubi rursus occurrit, quomodo quid hic ageretur Abraham pater ipse nesciebat, ubi sciebat esse Moysen et prophetas, id est libros eorum, quibus homines oboediendo tormenta inferna euitarent, ubi denique nouerat diuitem illum in deliciis, pauperem uero Lazarum in laboribus doloribusque uixisse. nam et hoc illi ait: memento, fili, quia percepisti bona in uita tua, Lazarus autem mala. sciebat ergo haec, quae utique apud uiuos, non apud mortuos gesta fuerant. uerum non cum agerentur in uiuis, sed eis mortuis potuit Lazaro indicante cognoscere, ne falsum sit, quod ait propheta: Abraham nesciuit nos.
thought_title: The rich man's request does not prove the dead know the living
orientation: Augustine is answering an objection from the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, arguing that the rich man cared about his living brothers without knowing what they were doing.
pass_a_gloss: Someone may say: if the dead have no care for the living, how did that rich man, who was being tormented in the underworld, ask father Abraham to send Lazarus to his five brothers not yet dead and to deal with them, so that they themselves may not also come into the same place of torments? But surely, because that rich man said this, did he therefore know what the brothers were doing or what they were suffering at that time? So he had care for the living, although he did not know at all what they were doing, just as we have care for the dead, although we certainly do not know what they are doing. For if we cared nothing about the dead, we would certainly not pray to God for them. Finally Abraham did not send Lazarus, and he answered that they have here Moses and the prophets, whom they ought to hear, so that they may not come to those punishments. Where again the question arises, how father Abraham himself did not know what was being done here, where he knew that Moses and the prophets were, that is their books, by obeying which people avoid the torments of the underworld, where finally he had learned that that rich man had lived in pleasures, but poor Lazarus in labors and pains. For he also says this to him: remember, son, that you received good things in your life, but Lazarus bad things. Therefore he knew these things, which certainly had been done among the living, not among the dead. But he was able to learn them not while they were being done among the living, but after they were dead, with Lazarus indicating them, so that it may not be false what the prophet says: Abraham did not know us.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'underworld' for inferi, avoiding 'hell' which would import a later theological sense.
The glossary gives 'prayer' for supplicatio; rendering the verb as 'pray' keeps the glossary term's sense.
Keeps the literal force of tormenta and the glossary rendering of inferi as underworld.
Literal rendering of the ablative phrase; 'delights' would be slightly more polished but 'pleasures' is plain and accurate.
Ablative absolute rendered literally to preserve the means by which Abraham learned.

pass_b_english: Someone may say: if the dead have no concern for the living, how is it that the rich man who was being tormented in the underworld asked father Abraham to send Lazarus to his five brothers who were not yet dead, to warn them, so that they would not also come into that same place of torments? But surely it does not follow that because that rich man said this, he knew what his brothers were doing or suffering at that time. He had concern for the living even though he had no idea what they were doing, just as we have concern for the dead even though we certainly do not know what they are doing. For if we had no concern for the dead, we would not pray to God for them. In the end Abraham did not send Lazarus, and he answered that they had Moses and the prophets here, whom they ought to obey so that they would not come to those punishments (Luke 16:29). Here again the question arises: how did father Abraham himself not know what was happening here, when he knew that Moses and the prophets were here—that is, their books, by obeying which people avoid the torments of the underworld—and when he also knew that the rich man had lived in pleasures while poor Lazarus had lived in labors and pains? For he says to him: “Remember, child, that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus in like manner evil things” (Luke 16:25). So he knew these things, which had certainly taken place among the living, not among the dead. But he could not have known them while they were happening among the living; he was able to learn them after they had died, with Lazarus indicating them—so that what the prophet says is not false: “Abraham did not know us” (Isaiah 63:16).

problems.quote: to deal with them so that they would not also come
problems.source_quote: et agat cum eis, ne ueniant et ipsi
problems.why: 'agat cum eis' means 'warn/admonish them,' not 'deal with them.'
problems.fix: to warn them, so that they would not also come
problems.ruling: 'agat cum eis' = 'deal/act with them' is too vague; context demands 'warn/admonish' (Luke 16:28 'testify').

problems.quote: he was able to learn them after they were dead
problems.source_quote: sed eis mortuis potuit Lazaro indicante cognoscere
problems.why: 'eis mortuis' = 'after they [the rich man and Lazarus] were dead', not 'after they [the things] were dead'; English misreads pronoun reference
problems.fix: he was able to learn them after they had died, with Lazarus indicating them
problems.ruling: 'eis mortuis' refers to persons (rich man and Lazarus), not events; 'after they were dead' misleads reader.

edits.old: to deal with them so that they would not also come
edits.new: to warn them, so that they would not also come

edits.old: he was able to learn them after they were dead, with Lazarus indicating them
edits.new: he was able to learn them after they had died, with Lazarus indicating them

fixed: Changed 'to deal with them' to 'to warn them' because 'agat cum eis' means to admonish or warn them, not merely to deal with them.
Changed 'after they were dead' to 'after they had died' because 'eis mortuis' refers to the rich man and Lazarus, not to the things that had taken place.

last_rejected.quote: whom they ought to obey so that they would not come to those punishments
last_rejected.source_quote: quos audire deberent, ut ad illa supplicia non uenirent
last_rejected.why: audire = 'hear/listen to', not 'obey'; oboediendo later is obey, but here it's 'listen to'.
last_rejected.fix: whom they ought to hear so that they would not come to those punishments
last_rejected.ruling: audire deberent = 'they ought to hear/listen to'; 'obey' stretches normal range but captures functional sense in context.

last_rejected.quote: by obeying which people avoid the torments of the underworld
last_rejected.source_quote: quibus homines oboediendo tormenta inferna euitarent
last_rejected.why: oboediendo is ablative gerund 'by obeying'; quibus is dative 'to which', not 'which' as object.
last_rejected.fix: by obedience to which people would avoid the torments of the underworld
last_rejected.ruling: quibus homines oboediendo = 'by obeying which [books]' is standard ablative of means; dative quibus with oboediendo is normal Latin construction.

last_rejected.quote: In the end Abraham did not send Lazarus
last_rejected.why: "denique" means "finally/lastly," not "in the end"; it introduces a concluding point, not a temporal conclusion.
last_rejected.fix: Finally, Abraham did not send Lazarus
last_rejected.ruling: "In the end" is a valid rendering of "denique" introducing a concluding point; no meaning is changed or lost.

last_rejected.quote: and he answered that they had Moses and the prophets here
last_rejected.source_quote: et Moysen ac prophetas hic eos habere respondit
last_rejected.why: The Latin says Abraham "answered that they had Moses and the prophets here," not "he answered that they had." The English makes "he answered" a separate clause, distorting the syntax and making it seem like Abraham's response was only about possession, not about listening to them.
last_rejected.fix: and answered that they had Moses and the prophets here
last_rejected.ruling: English accurately renders "eos habere respondit" as "answered that they had"; syntax and meaning are preserved.

last_rejected.quote: But he could not have known them while they were happening among the living; he was able to learn them after they had died, with Lazarus indicating them
last_rejected.source_quote: uerum non cum agerentur in uiuis, sed eis mortuis potuit Lazaro indicante cognoscere
last_rejected.why: "eis mortuis" means "when they [the people involved] had died," not "after they [the subjects] had died." The English "after they had died" is ambiguous and could mislead; more importantly, "eis" refers to the people whose lives were being lived (the rich man and Lazarus), not to "these things" (haec). The Latin says he learned after those people died, not after "things" died.
last_rejected.fix: But he could not have known them while they were happening among the living; he was able to learn them once those people had died, with Lazarus indicating them
last_rejected.ruling: "After they had died" correctly renders "eis mortuis"; pronoun reference is clear from context, no real error.
